Context/Background: Perianal fistulizing Crohn’s disease (CD) is a severe gastrointestinal disorder causing extensive mucosal damage with limited treatment options. Severe manifestations of the disease appear at higher rates in non-Europeans but the genetic and cellular mechanisms driving the disease phenotypes remain poorly understood. Herein, we tested whether pathologic determinants in the epithelial stem cell compartment could be detected at the transcript level in rectal organoids derived from a diverse patient population. Rectal organoid and mucosal cells from endoscopic biopsies of each patient having perianal fistulizing CD or no disease controls were prepared for and sequenced at the single cell level. After cell type annotations based on expressed marker genes, samples were analyzed by principal components, for differential transcript expression, cell type proportions, and pathway enrichment.
Prompt: To assess differences in pathway activity based on transcription profiles between the mucosa epithelial cells and the corresponding patient derived organoids, we calculated pathway enrichment scores for paired Mucosa vs Organoids.  Please give a summary of the pathway enrichment results.  Focus on highlighting similarities and differences in the UP (Mucosa enriched) and DOWN (Organoid enriched) pathways.

Introduction/Context  
We compared Reactome pathway enrichments between paired mucosal epithelial cells (“Mucosa-enriched,” UP) and patient-derived rectal organoids (“Organoid-enriched,” DOWN) from perianal fistulizing Crohn’s disease vs. control biopsies. Differential expression within each pair yielded 693 significant Reactome terms (FDR-adjusted), 412 UP (genes higher in mucosa) and 281 DOWN (genes higher in organoids). For DOWN pathways we report only those with GeneCount ≤6 (Organoid-enriched); for UP we highlight the top categories by GeneCount.  

Keywords  
• Vesicle transport  
• Membrane trafficking  
• RHO GTPase signaling  
• DNA repair / cell cycle  
• Metabolism  

Candidate Genes  
• CFTR (vesicle transport)  
• EGFR (trafficking, signaling)  
• CDK1 (cell cycle)  
• APEX1 (DNA repair)  
• FADS2 (lipid metabolism)  

Pathway Enrichments  

UP (Mucosa-enriched) (top 10 by GeneCount)  
| Theme                                       | GeneCount | Leading Genes (examples)                 |  
|---------------------------------------------|-----------|------------------------------------------|  
| Vesicle-mediated transport                  | 224       | CFTR, RAB27A, EGFR, AKT1, AP1G1          |  
| Infectious disease                          | 222       | CASP1, STAT1, NFKB1, B2M, EGFR           |  
| Membrane trafficking                        | 222       | CFTR, RAB27A, EGFR, AP1B1, SNAP23        |  
| Signaling by RHO GTPases, MIRO, RHOBTB3     | 215       | VAV3, CDC42EP5, RHOA, WASL, PIK3CA       |  
| Signaling by RHO GTPases                    | 207       | VAV3, CDC42EP5, RHOA, WASL, PIK3CA       |  
| Metabolism of RNA                           | 193       | PRKCD, DDX5, SMG1, UPF1, XRN1            |  
| Cellular responses to stimuli               | 192       | NFKB1, CREBBP, MTOR, HIF1AN, AKT1        |  
| Cellular responses to stress                | 185       | NFKB1, CREBBP, MTOR, HIF1AN, AKT1        |  
| Metabolism of lipids                        | 174       | FADS2, CPT1A, PPARGC1A, ACADM, GPAT4     |  
| RHO GTPase cycle                            | 157       | VAV3, CDC42EP5, RHOA, PAK4, SOS1         |  

DOWN (Organoid-enriched) (all GeneCount ≤6)  
| Theme                                      | GeneCount | Leading Genes                      |  
|--------------------------------------------|-----------|-----------------------------------|  
| Activation of NIMA kinases NEK9, NEK6, NEK7 | 4         | CCNB1, CDK1, NEK6                 |  
| Aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling       | 4         | AHR, HSP90AB1                     |  
| Displacement of DNA glycosylase by APEX1   | 4         | APEX1, MPG                        |  
| Fructose metabolism                        | 4         | SORD, KHK                         |  
| Formation of xylulose-5-phosphate          | 4         | SORD, DCXR                        |  
| Phosphorylation of EMI1                    | 4         | CCNB1, CDK1                       |  
| POLB-dependent long patch base excision    | 4         | POLB, FEN1, APEX1                |  
| Reversal of alkylation damage by dioxygenases | 4     | ALKBH2, ALKBH3                    |  
| DNA damage reversal                        | 5         | MGMT, ALKBH5                      |  
| Folding of actin by CCT TRiC               | 5         | ACTB, CCT8                        |  
| Linoleic acid metabolism                   | 5         | FADS1, ELOVL5                     |  
| Receptor-mediated mitophagy                | 5         | ULK1, MAP1LC3B                    |  
| Regulation of BACH1 activity               | 5         | SKP1, SKP2                        |  
| SEMA4D-mediated inhibition of cell migration | 5      | RHOA, RAC1                        |  
| SUMO is conjugated to E1 (UBA2:SAE1)       | 5         | SUMO1–3, SAE1                     |  
| Vitamin C metabolism                       | 5         | SLC2A1, CYB5R3                    |  
| Mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis | 6       | ISCA1, GLRX5                      |  
| Nucleotide biosynthesis                     | 6        | IMPDH1, GMPS                      |  
| Processing & activation of SUMO            | 6         | SUMO1–3, UBE2I                   |  
| Purine catabolism                           | 6        | NT5E, PNP                        |  

Analysis  
Mucosal cells are broadly enriched for vesicle- and membrane-trafficking pathways, RHO GTPase-driven cytoskeletal dynamics, immune/infection responses, RNA metabolism, stress signaling, lipid processing, transcription/chromatin regulation, and antigen presentation. In contrast, organoids show a narrow set of enriched pathways, predominantly focused on cell-cycle kinase activation (CCNB1/CDK1/NEK kinases), DNA repair (base excision and damage reversal), specific metabolic routes (fructose, linoleic acid, vitamin C), sumoylation, mitophagy, and mitochondrial iron-sulfur assembly.  

Mucosa and organoids both engage metabolism (e.g., RNA, lipids) and stress responses, but mucosa shows greater diversity and higher overall gene counts. Organoids preferentially up-regulate genome maintenance, cell-cycle checkpoints, and niche-specific metabolic enzymes, suggesting a shift toward proliferative and housekeeping programs ex vivo.  

These contrasts underscore that organoids recapitulate fundamental epithelial homeostasis yet lack the extensive vesicular trafficking and immune-coupled signaling characteristic of native mucosa.
